summary: Specifies a packetization scheme for carrying uncompressed video in RTP. It supports a range of standard- and high-definition formats, including television formats such as ITU BT.601 and SMPTE standards. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Video is a stack of pictures. This memo cuts raw, uncompressed pictures into chunks small enough to mail over the internet and shows how to put them back together.

subtitle: How to chop studio-quality raw video into RTP packets, scan line by scan line, and put it back together.

tldr.problem: Uncompressed, studio-quality video (standard and high definition) needs a way to travel in RTP packets, even though its formats come in many sizes, color layouts and sample depths.
tldr.mechanism: Each scan line is cut into whole pixel groups and sent in one or more RTP packets. A small payload header per line carries a 16-bit sequence number extension, the line number, the pixel offset and a continuation flag.
tldr.outcome: A single flexible scheme covers YCbCr, RGB and related formats at varying data rates. The RFC warns that the bandwidth is huge, so senders must watch packet loss. It is updated by RFC 4421.

today: RFC 4175 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4421; read the two together. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4175 defines a way to packetize uncompressed, studio-quality video for the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). It covers formats such as ITU-R BT.601 (standard definition, 625-line and 525-line), SMPTE 274M (1920x1080, progressive or interlaced) and SMPTE 296M (1280x720, progressive).

The authors observe that these formats differ in detail but are structurally very similar, so one payload format can carry them and other similar formats. It is a Standards Track document.
sections.eli5: Big TV studios use pictures that have not been squished down at all. This memo is the shipping label that lets those pictures travel over the internet.

sections.title: Payload Design
sections.content:
Each scan line is packetized into one or more RTP packets. If a whole line is larger than the network MTU, it SHOULD be fragmented into several packets, each smaller than the MTU. One packet MAY also carry more than one line. Only active samples go in the payload; blanking intervals and inactive samples SHOULD NOT be sent.

Scan line numbers travel in the payload header, together with a field identifier for interlaced video. In progressive scanning, lines are shown top to bottom as a full frame. In interlaced scanning, a frame is split into two fields of odd and even lines. For SMPTE 296M, valid line numbers are 26 through 745. For progressive SMPTE 274M they are 42 through 1121.

The 16-bit RTP sequence number would wrap very quickly at high rates: the RFC computes about 0.5 seconds for a 1-Gbps stream with packets of at least 1000 octets. The payload header therefore adds a 16-bit extension, giving a 32-bit sequence number with a wrap-around time of approximately nine hours.

Ancillary data such as audio or time code SHOULD be delivered in separate RTP sessions that run at the same time, synchronized with normal RTP mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Each row of dots goes in its own envelope, or in several envelopes if the row is too long. The envelopes get a longer counting number so the numbers do not run out while a very fast video is sent.

sections.title: RTP Packetization and Headers
sections.content:
The standard RTP header is followed by a 2-octet payload header holding the Extended Sequence Number, then by a 6-octet header for each line (or partial line) of video included, and then the video data. With one line or fragment per packet, the headers stay 32-bit aligned.

Each line header has: Length (16 bits, octets of data from this line, which MUST be a multiple of the pgroup size), F (1 bit, which field; always 0 for progressive video), Line No (15 bits), C (1 bit, set to 1 if another line header follows) and Offset (15 bits, the pixel offset of the first pixel in the payload within the line).

The fixed RTP header keeps its usual meaning with a few notes. The payload type is dynamically allocated. The timestamp is the sampling instant of the frame (progressive) or field (interlaced), a 90-kHz timestamp SHOULD be used, and packets MUST NOT mix data from different frames or fields. The marker bit MUST be 1 on the last packet of a frame or field and 0 otherwise.
sections.eli5: Every envelope has a small note on it: which row, how far along the row the first dot is, how many dots there are, and whether another row is also inside. The last envelope of a picture gets a special mark.

sections.title: Pixel Groups and Sample Packing
sections.content:
Samples may be 8, 10, 12 or 16 bits. Pixels that share color samples (color sub-sampling, typical in YCbCr) MUST travel together as a pixel group, or pgroup: the smallest group of pixels that is a whole number of octets and in which shared samples stay inside the group. Video data MUST NOT be fragmented within a pgroup.

Packing order depends on the format: Red-Green-Blue for RGB, Blue-Green-Red for BGR, Cb-Y-Cr for YCbCr 4:4:4, Cb0-Y0-Cr0-Y1 for 4:2:2, and Cb0-Y0-Y1-Cr0-Y2-Y3 for 4:1:1. For 4:2:0, progressive video sends samples from two consecutive lines in one packet, with the line number of the first line of the pair.

If a line does not end on a pgroup boundary, the sender MUST fill the rest of the last pgroup with zero bits and the receiver MUST ignore them. Chrominance samples may be placed between luminance samples or co-sited with them; this does not change packing order but must be signaled to the receiver for interpolation.
sections.eli5: Some dots share their color with their neighbors, like friends sharing one crayon. Friends who share must always ride in the same envelope, so the envelope is always filled with whole groups of friends.

sections.title: Media Type Parameters and SDP
sections.content:
The IANA registration is media type video/raw. The required parameters are rate (RTP clock rate, 90000 recommended), sampling (RGB, RGBA, BGR, BGRA, YCbCr-4:4:4, YCbCr-4:2:2, YCbCr-4:2:0 or YCbCr-4:1:1), width and height (each 1 to 32767), depth (bits per sample) and colorimetry (BT601-5, BT709-2 or SMPTE240M).

Optional parameters include interlace, top-field-first, chroma-position (0 to 8) and gamma. New sampling and colorimetry values can be registered under the Specification Required policy. In SDP, the parameters are copied into the a=fmtp line as semicolon-separated pairs. Because the sample size and data type are signaled out of band, the receiver learns them from this description, not from the packets.
sections.eli5: Before the video starts, the sender sends a description card: how wide and tall the picture is, how many colors per dot, and how the colors are shared. The envelopes themselves do not repeat this.

sections.title: Security and Bandwidth Considerations
sections.content:
RTP packets in this format are subject to the security considerations of RTP and the RTP profile in use, which implies that confidentiality is achieved by encryption. The format does not show significant non-uniformity in receiver processing cost that could enable a denial of service.

The larger concern is bandwidth: the RFC cites up to 270 Mbps for standard-definition video and approximately 1 Gbps for high-definition video, enough to cause denial of service on most Internet paths. If best-effort service is used, users MUST monitor packet loss. Loss is acceptable if a TCP flow on the same path would get an average throughput not less than the RTP flow is getting. Senders can meet this with congestion control, or receivers can leave the session if loss is too high.

On networks with quality-of-service guarantees, receivers SHOULD monitor loss and, if the service is not delivered, behave as under best effort. RTCP SHOULD be used per RFC 3550, but the sender octet count and cumulative loss fields wrap quickly at these rates, so other means of tracking them SHOULD be used.
sections.eli5: Raw video is like a firehose. If you point it at a small garden hose, everyone suffers, so senders must notice when pieces are getting lost and slow down.

sections.title: Relation to RFC 2431 and RFC 3497
sections.content:
Compared with RFC 2431, this memo supports more frame sizes, color sub-sampling schemes and sample sizes. It handles up to 32768 scan lines and pixels per line, while BT.656 can carry up to 4096 lines and 2048 pixels per line. RFC 2431 addresses only 4:2:2 YCbCr and signals in band; this memo covers YCbCr, RGB, RGBA, BGR and BGRA and assumes out-of-band signaling.

RFC 3497 is a circuit emulation of SMPTE 292M at a fixed 1.485 Gbps and transports blanking. This memo is a native packetization for any uncompressed video at varying data rates and transports only active pixels.
sections.eli5: Older memos handled one kind of video, or copied a whole studio cable exactly. This one is a more general box that fits many kinds of video and only packs the picture itself.

fields.name: Extended Sequence Number
fields.desc: High-order 16 bits of the 32-bit sequence number.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets of data from this line; a multiple of the pgroup size.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Field identification; 0 for the first field and for progressive video.

fields.name: Line No
fields.desc: Scan line number of the encapsulated data.

fields.name: Offset
fields.desc: Pixel offset of the first pixel of the payload within the line.
